CruiseMapper currently has no ship schedule for Port Alang Ship Breaking Yard (India)

Alang (port locode INALA) is a small "port" town in India's Gujarat State (Saurashtra Region, Bhavnagar District) with population around 20,000. Since the early 1990s, Alang has been worldwide known for its shipbreaking yard (the world's largest). There, retired marine vessels (cargo and passenger) are beached/grounded then dismantled. Some vessels (without their own power) are towed.

The 1983-founded Alang Yard is also officially classified as "Port Alang" and dubbed "Alang Ship Breaking Port". Here, ~50% of the world's salvaged ships have been dismantled and recycled (a total of 153 shipbreaking plots), making it the largest ship graveyard on the planet. The beaches where the vessels are broken up are on the Gulf of Khambhat, approx 50 km (31 mi) southeast of the district's capital city (Bhavnagar). Approx 175 km (110 mi) southwest of Alang is Diu Island. Approx 280 km (170 mi) to the south is Mumbai (Bombay) - direct/sea distance.

At Alang's beaches are dismantled all types of vessels, including oil-gas tankers, boxships (container carriers), bulk-cargo carriers, Ro-Ro (car ferries), passenger ships (ferries and cruise liners), and naval ships. The vessels are beached during high tide. When the tide recedes, hundreds of workers start to break up each ship. Most of the machinery and furniture are salvaged, and the rest is for scrap. The work is hard and dangerous, with numerous serious injuries (even deaths) happening daily.

There are plans to modernize the Alang Shipyard since India and Japan signed an MoU (Memorandum of Understanding) for technology and financial help from Japan. The public-private partnership aims to upgrade Alang's shipbreaking and recycling operations according to the latest international safety-, health- and environmental regulations, as well as to make it IMO-compliant.

The Yard's largest vessel so far is the supertanker "MS Seawise Giant" (oil tanker, IMO 7381154, 1979-built, 2010-scrapped as "MS Mont"). This was also the world's longest ship - with LOA length 459 m (1504 ft), draft 25 m (81 ft), GT 260941 tons, DWT 564763 tons.

Note: Due to the Coronavirus crisis and IMO's new regulations (marine engine upgrades for using low-sulfur fuels and LNG), in 2020-2021 were scrapped 15 cruise liners - an unprecedented number in comparison to previous years, and even 5-year periods. In 2020, the average ship scrap metal (DWT-deadweight tonnage) prices in Alang rose to ~USD 400 per ton (from ~$200), in Aliaga - to ~USD 300 per ton (from ~$100). EU-flagged ships' scrap values were ~USD 100-200 per ton as these vessels require dismantling at EU-certified yards. Ship scrap prices in the USA were USD 80-90 per ton.

Next video is the 70-min long Canadian documentary film (by Michael Kot) titled "Shipbreakers" (2004) focusing on Alang Yard's deplorable working conditions.

 

Currently, the world's top-4 largest shipbreaking yards are Alang (India), Chittagong (Bangladesh), Gadani (Pakistan), Aliaga (Turkey). For CruiseMapper's collection of destroyed cruise liners see our Scrapped Cruise Ships.

Alang is not a conventional cruise port. It is a specialist ship-recycling destination on the Gulf of Khambhat, where end-of-life vessels normally anchor offshore and are then beached at recycling plots. No regular cruise passenger terminal or walk-off sightseeing area is documented, and CruiseMapper currently lists no scheduled cruise calls.

Independent sightseeing limited or not recommended. Any passenger landing or shore access on a special call would need to be arranged through the ship and its local agent. Once ashore, a pre-arranged car with driver is the practical way to explore the area.

Getting from the Port

  • Cruise terminal: There is no conventional passenger cruise terminal documented at Alang.
  • Walking: The recycling zone is an active industrial area and is not suitable for casual independent walking.
  • Shuttles: Do not assume that a cruise shuttle will be available; arrangements for any special passenger call would be ship-specific.
  • Road transport: A private car or taxi arranged in advance is the most practical option.
  • Bhavnagar: approximately 50 km (31.1 mi) from Alang, normally around 45–60 minutes by road depending on traffic and the exact starting point.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Visit the Alang-Sosiya Ship Recycling Yard

This is the main reason to visit Alang, but it is not a normal sightseeing attraction. Gujarat Maritime Board allows visits by Indian and foreign visitors subject to permission from the Port Officer. Arrange permission before the visit rather than expecting to enter on arrival.

Photography and videography inside the ship-recycling yard are prohibited for security, safety and environmental reasons. Visitors should remain with authorized escorts and follow all instructions because this is a working heavy-industrial site.

Allow: roughly 2–3 hours once local transport and access arrangements are included. Best for: maritime and industrial-interest visitors. Independent visit: not suitable without prior authorization.

Bhavnagar City

For passengers who have several hours ashore, Bhavnagar provides a more conventional sightseeing option. The city is approximately 50 km (31.1 mi) from Alang, so allow about 1.5–2 hours for the return drive plus sightseeing time.

Takhteshwar Temple is a practical short stop, reached by steps to a hilltop overlooking the city. Victoria Park provides a contrasting green area near Gaurishankar Lake if time permits.

Allow: about 4–5 hours including transfers. Independent visit: possible with a pre-arranged driver. Avoid relying on connections between local buses during a time-limited call.

Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill

Palitana is approximately 53 km (32.9 mi) by road from Alang. Its Shatrunjaya Hill temple complex is one of Gujarat's major sights, but reaching the principal temples requires climbing more than 3,700 stone steps. The ascent alone can take around two hours.

This is a demanding full excursion rather than a quick side trip. Allow at least 5–7 hours for driving, climbing and time among the temples, and considerably more flexibility in hot weather.

Difficulty: challenging. Independent visit: possible with a private driver on a long port call, but an organized or pre-arranged excursion is preferable because of the distance and substantial walking time.

Walking Around Alang

A self-guided walking tour is not recommended. The coastline is occupied by active ship-recycling plots spread along an industrial zone, and access to the yards is controlled. There is no practical route from a cruise passenger exit linking conventional attractions on foot.

Practical Tips

  • Confirm shore landing arrangements with the ship before making independent plans; Alang should not be treated like a normal cruise terminal.
  • Arrange a vehicle and driver in advance for any trip beyond the immediate Alang area.
  • Obtain Gujarat Maritime Board permission beforehand if the ship-recycling yard itself is the objective.
  • Do not plan to photograph or film inside the recycling yard.
  • Allow extra time for industrial traffic and road delays around Alang.
  • For trips to Bhavnagar or Palitana, plan to be back at the arranged ship or landing point at least 60–90 minutes before the required all-aboard time, with a larger margin if tendering or other special transfer procedures are involved.
